title: SSD-native search and the I/O that dominates
summary: A hundred reads per query means 63 percent of queries touch the device's p99, so you need its p99.99 rather than its p99. Measured and simulated, planning from the median under-predicts the median query by 40 percent and the p99 query by nearly three times.
html:
Yesterday's latency arithmetic multiplied a hop count by a datasheet number. Every term in that calculation is optimistic, and today is about by how much.

You never read what you asked for

The node record from Day 25 is 1,796 bytes. You cannot read 1,796 bytes:

record 1796 B over a 4 KB OS page     ->  4,096 B read   2.28x
record straddling a 4 KB boundary     ->  8,192 B read   4.56x
record over a 16 KB flash page        -> 16,384 B read   9.12x

The first row is unavoidable and fine. The second is an alignment bug: if your records are packed back to back rather than aligned to the page, a good fraction of them cross a boundary and silently cost two reads. Pad to the page.

The third row is the one people miss. Your OS issues a 4 KB read, but flash is organised in pages that are commonly 16 KB, so the device may have to fetch 16 KB internally to serve you 4 KB. The amplification you measure at the filesystem is not the amplification the device performs, and the gap matters for endurance and for throughput under load.

Latency is a distribution, not a number

Here is a real measurement. 8,000 random 4 KB reads with O_DIRECT against a 256 MB file on this machine:

p50     0.9 us
p99     3.6 us      4x the median
p99.9  66.1 us     73x the median
max   115.8 us    129x the median

Read the absolute numbers with suspicion. A 0.9 microsecond median is not flash, it is almost certainly the hypervisor's page cache answering on the device's behalf, which is what usually happens to O_DIRECT inside a VM. Take the shape and ignore the scale: a tight median, and a tail that is nearly two orders of magnitude worse. Real NVMe shows the same shape with a worse tail, because garbage collection, wear levelling and read disturb all produce occasional very slow reads.

Why a tail you could ignore becomes a tail you cannot

One read lands in the p99 tail one percent of the time. Nobody cares. But a graph search does a hundred reads, and it is only as fast as the slowest one it waited on:

P(at least one read lands in the tail)

 reads    p99 tail   p99.9 tail   p99.99 tail
     1        1.0%         0.1%          0.0%
    10        9.6%         1.0%          0.1%
   100       63.4%         9.5%          1.0%
   200       86.6%        18.1%          2.0%

At a hundred reads per query, 63 percent of your queries touch the device's p99. Your typical query is living in the device's tail.

Turn it around and the requirement is stark:

to keep 99% of QUERIES clean, the single-read tail must be below:

 n=10 reads  ->  you need the device's p99.9
 n=100       ->  you need the device's p99.99
 n=200       ->  you need the device's p99.995

A device chosen on its p99 is the wrong device. Fan-out converts a rare event into a common one, and the exponent is your hop count.

What this does to the estimate

I took the measured distribution and simulated a 100-read query by drawing from it:

naive estimate, 100 x median      91.4 us
simulated query p50              124.7 us    1.4x the estimate
simulated query p99              266.7 us    2.9x
simulated query max              382.3 us    4.2x

queries exceeding 2x the naive estimate:  15.0%

Planning from the median under-predicts the median query by 40 percent and the p99 query by nearly three times. And this is on a distribution whose tail is mild compared to a real SSD under write pressure.

If you size a system by multiplying hops by a datasheet latency, you will be wrong in the direction that gets noticed.

The write path you forgot about

One more term, and it is the one that catches people who tested on a quiet machine. Your index is not only being read. Documents arrive, vectors get written, and on flash a write is never just a write.

Flash cannot overwrite a page in place. The controller writes elsewhere, marks the old page dead, and later a garbage collector copies the surviving pages out of a block so the block can be erased. That copying is write amplification, and while it is happening your reads queue behind it.

Which gives you a nasty coupling: your retrieval tail latency is a function of your ingest rate. A system that is comfortably fast during a read-only benchmark can miss its latency budget during a bulk reindex, and nothing in the retrieval code changed. If you have ever watched a database's p99 degrade during compaction, this is that, one layer down.

The practical consequence is that the benchmark worth running is reads and writes together, at your real ingest rate, and the capacity question is not "how fast is my storage" but "how fast is my storage while it is also absorbing my pipeline".

What to do about it

Do fewer reads. The only robust fix, because every other mitigation fights the exponent instead of reducing it. Cache the nodes near the entry point in RAM: the first few hops of every search traverse the same small set, so a few hundred megabytes of hot nodes removes a third of the reads for free. DiskANN does exactly this.

Make each read count. Align records to page boundaries. If several nodes are usually traversed together, pack them into the same page so one read serves several hops. This is graph partitioning for locality, and it is the same problem as choosing a clustered index.

Keep the queue deep. Day 25's point, with a second reason behind it: concurrency hides tail latency as well as serialisation, because a slow read overlaps with the others rather than stalling behind them.

Measure your own device, under load. An idle benchmark tells you almost nothing about a device that is also absorbing writes from your ingest pipeline. The tail you care about is the one that appears when garbage collection is running, which is exactly when you are least likely to be benchmarking.

The honest limits of today

I measured a virtualised disk in a container and the median is not credible as flash. What I would stand behind: the probability arithmetic, which is just arithmetic, and the shape of the distribution, which I have never seen a storage device fail to exhibit. The simulation combines those two, so it inherits the same confidence.

What I cannot tell you is your own numbers. Nobody can, which is why exercise three yesterday was to run fio, and why doing it under a realistic write load is worth more than any figure in this lesson.

Phase 2 has spent six days making vectors smaller and six making them findable. Tomorrow returns to compression with the simplest idea in it, which turns out to be competitive with the sophisticated one: scalar and binary quantization.
exercise:
1. Compute your own fan-out exponent. Take your expected hops per query, call it n, and compute 1 - (1 - p)^n for p of 0.01 and 0.001. That gives the fraction of your queries that will touch the device's p99 and p99.9. If the first number is above about 20 percent, your query latency is a tail-latency problem and tuning the median will not help.

2. Check your record alignment. Work out your node record size, then whether consecutive records in your layout cross 4 KB boundaries. Compute what fraction do. Every one of those is a doubled read, and padding to the page costs you only the slack bytes.

3. Measure under load, not at rest. Run a 4 KB random read benchmark on your real storage twice: once idle, and once with a sustained sequential write running alongside it. Compare the p99 and p99.9 of both. The second pair is what your queries will actually see in production, and the difference is usually larger than people expect.
